title: GOBAI: the oxygen minimum zone of the eastern tropical North Pacific
text:
Map the oxygen minimum zone off Mexico and Central America, and track how far it reaches, every week from 1993 to 2025, from NOAA’s GOBAI HR (Gridded Ocean Biogeochemistry from Artificial Intelligence): dissolved oxygen on a ¼° grid, 58 pressure levels, weekly.
The product is 1,719 weekly fields per variable, in netCDF files of 1.4–7.3 GB each on Google Cloud. The virtual Icechunk store makes them one dataset. No credentials needed.

title: GOBAI: the oxygen minimum zone of the eastern tropical North Pacific
text:
The textbook idea
Below the sunlit surface, bacteria use up oxygen as they break down sinking organic matter, and only circulation brings more. In the eastern tropical Pacific, high productivity at the surface meets slow, old water at depth, and oxygen at a few hundred metres falls almost to zero: an oxygen minimum zone (OMZ). Below about 60 µmol/kg (≈ 2 mg/L) many fish and invertebrates are stressed (hypoxic); below about 20 µmol/kg most animals cannot live. Tropical OMZs have expanded over recent decades (Stramma et al. 2008).
GOBAI HR is preliminary, and it is a machine-learning estimate from temperature, salinity and sparse oxygen observations, not a measurement at each point.

title: GOBAI: the oxygen minimum zone of the eastern tropical North Pacific
text:
Read 33 years at 300 dbar
Every week from 1993 to 2025, one pressure level (300 dbar, about 300 m), 5 °S–40 °N and 160–75 °W. The store’s chunks are 100 weeks × one level × a 45° tile, so this is about 100 chunks; it took about a minute on a JupyterHub in AWS, and should be faster on Colab, which runs in Google Cloud next to the data.

o2 = ds.o2.sel(mean_pressure=300, latitude=slice(-5, 40), longitude=slice(200, 285))
o2 = o2.assign_coords(longitude=o2.longitude - 360)        # 0–360 to −180–180

start = time.time()
o2 = o2.load()
print(f"{o2.time.size:,} weeks read in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")

1,719 weeks read in 6 s

title: GOBAI: the oxygen minimum zone of the eastern tropical North Pacific
text:
Map: mean oxygen at 300 dbar

mean = o2.mean("time")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
ax.set_facecolor("0.85")                                     # land
mean.plot(ax=ax, cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=250, cbar_kwargs={"label": "O₂ at 300 dbar (µmol/kg)"})
cs = mean.plot.contour(ax=ax, levels=[20, 60], colors=["w", "r"], linewidths=1.5)
ax.clabel(cs, fmt="%d")
ax.axvline(-130, color="k", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set(title="GOBAI HR mean dissolved oxygen at 300 dbar, 1993–2025 (red: 60, white: 20 µmol/kg)",
       xlabel="longitude", ylabel="latitude")
plt.show()








The white 20 µmol/kg line encloses the core of the zone, a tongue reaching west from Mexico and Central America to about 145 °W; the northern edge of its southern counterpart, off Peru, shows at the bottom. The red 60 µmol/kg line, the edge of hypoxic water, runs much further north along the coast, up Baja California and California, where the California Undercurrent carries low-oxygen water poleward.

title: GOBAI: the oxygen minimum zone of the eastern tropical North Pacific
text:
Extent through time
Two measures, one value per week, averaged by year: the area below 60 µmol/kg in the box, and the northern edge of that water along 130 °W (the dotted line on the map), far enough offshore that the coast does not get in the way.

cell_km2 = (111.32 * 0.25) ** 2 * np.cos(np.deg2rad(o2.latitude))   # ¼° cells shrink toward the pole
hypoxic = o2 < 60
area = (hypoxic * cell_km2).sum(["latitude", "longitude"]) / 1e6        # million km²
edge = o2.latitude.where(hypoxic.sel(longitude=-130, method="nearest")).max("latitude")

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 6), sharex=True)
area.groupby("time.year").mean().plot(ax=ax1, marker="o")
ax1.set(xlabel="", ylabel="million km²", title="Area below 60 µmol/kg at 300 dbar")
edge.groupby("time.year").mean().plot(ax=ax2, marker="o", color="tab:red")
ax2.set(xlabel="year", ylabel="latitude (°N)", title="Northern edge of < 60 µmol/kg water along 130 °W")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








In GOBAI, the area below 60 µmol/kg at 300 dbar grew from 21.3 to 22.6 million km² (about 6 %) between 1993 and 2025, and along 130 °W its northern edge moved from about 18.9 °N to 20.7 °N, roughly 200 km. That is the direction of the expansion Stramma et al. reported. But GOBAI HR is preliminary, and oxygen observations were sparse in the early years, so treat this as something to check against observations, not as a result.
More: the GOBAI page has the viewer, ERDDAP access and how to cite GOBAI; GOBAI HR has no citable release yet.

title: OISST: world sea surface temperature since 1981
text:
Rebuild the well-known Climate Reanalyzer chart of daily world sea surface temperature from NOAA’s OISST v2.1: the area-weighted mean from 60 °S to 60 °N, one line per year.
The data are NOAA’s daily files on AWS, one NetCDF per day, about 16,500 of them. The virtual Icechunk store, maintained by NERACOOS / GMRI, makes them one dataset with one time axis, so the whole record is a single sel() and mean(). No credentials needed.

title: OISST: world sea surface temperature since 1981
text:
Average every 7th day, 60 °S to 60 °N
Each daily chunk in NOAA’s files is the whole global map, so the cost is one file per day read. Every 7th day keeps all 45 years and reads about 2,400 files, which took about 40 s on a 4-core JupyterHub in AWS (elsewhere, including Colab, expect longer). Set step = 1 to read all 16,500 files: about 5 minutes there. Dask streams the maps 8 at a time, so memory stays near 1 GB. The last couple of weeks are NOAA’s preliminary values.

step = 7                                        # set to 1 for every day (~5 min)
sst = daily.sst.squeeze("zlev").sel(lat=slice(-60, 60)).isel(time=slice(None, None, step))
sst = sst.chunk({"time": 8})
weights = np.cos(np.deg2rad(sst.lat))          # grid cells shrink toward the poles

start = time.time()
world = sst.weighted(weights).mean(["lat", "lon"]).compute()
print(f"{world.time.size:,} daily files read in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")

2,359 daily files read in 37 s

title: OISST: world sea surface temperature since 1981
text:
One line per year

df = world.to_dataframe(name="sst")
df["year"], df["doy"] = df.index.year, df.index.day_of_year
this_year = df.year.max()
years = range(1982, this_year + 1)               # 1981 starts in September: skip it
highlight = {2023: "tab:orange", 2024: "tab:red", this_year: "k"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
cmap = plt.cm.Blues
for y in years:
    one = df[df.year == y]
    if y in highlight:
        ax.plot(one.doy, one.sst, color=highlight[y], lw=2.5, label=str(y), zorder=3)
    else:
        ax.plot(one.doy, one.sst, color=cmap(0.25 + 0.75 * (y - 1982) / (this_year - 1 - 1982)), lw=0.8)
base = df[(df.year >= 1991) & (df.year <= 2020)]
clim = base.groupby(base.doy // 7 * 7 + 3).sst.mean()   # mean by week of the year
ax.plot(clim.index, clim, "k--", lw=1.5, label="1991–2020 mean")
ax.set(xlabel="day of year", ylabel="sea surface temperature (°C)", xlim=(1, 366),
       title=f"Daily world SST, 60 °S–60 °N (NOAA OISST v2.1); blue: 1982 (light) to {this_year - 1} (dark)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.show()








Each line is one year. The blue lines climb steadily: years in the 1980s average about 20.05 °C, the 2010s about 20.5 °C. In 2023 (orange) the ocean jumped above every earlier year, and it has stayed there: 2023 through 2026 each average about 0.5–0.65 °C above the 1991–2020 mean. 2026 (black, through mid-November) is running warmest of all. Reading every day (step = 1) finds the warmest day in the record so far: 21.18 °C on 26 August 2026.
This is the chart Climate Reanalyzer publishes, from the same OISST v2.1 data, rebuilt here from 16,500 files with one mean().
More: the store’s monthly/ group holds monthly means already computed and chunked for long time series, which is far cheaper when monthly is enough; see the store’s README.

Read profiles at Station ALOHA
One profile per month, 2009–2020: the 15th at 12Z (02:00 in Hawaiʻi, so the afternoon warm skin is not in it), top 1,500 m, temperature and salinity. Each chunk in this store is one depth level at one time step, so this is 144 times × 27 levels × 2 variables ≈ 7,800 reads, about 1.8 GB. That took about 15 s on a JupyterHub in AWS us-west-2.

aloha = (ds[["temp", "salt"]]

title: PacIOOS: seasons and water masses at Station ALOHA
section: Seasons reach only the top ~100 m
text:
Seasons reach only the top ~100 m
Sun and wind warm and stir the top of the ocean, so its temperature follows the seasons. Deeper down, the thermocline is shielded from them. Plot temperature at four depths through the 12 years.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
aloha.temp.sel(depth=[0.25, 50, 100, 200]).plot.line(ax=ax, x="time", hue="depth")
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="temperature (°C)", title="Temperature at Station ALOHA, one profile per month")
plt.show()








The surface swings about 4 °C each year, coolest in March and warmest in September. At 50 m the swing is nearly as large and peaks a month later, as the summer heat is mixed down. At 100 and 200 m the seasonal cycle is only about 1 °C. What you see there instead is irregular: eddies passing ALOHA move the thermocline up and down by tens of metres, which at 200 m changes the temperature by 2–4 °C.
crumbs: 2 · PacIOOS: seasons and water masses at ALOHA

title: PacIOOS: seasons and water masses at Station ALOHA
text:
Water masses in the profile
Below the mixed layer, salinity tells you where the water came from:

a salinity maximum near 75–100 m: North Pacific Tropical Water, salty water formed under the evaporation-dominated subtropical gyre to the northeast, that sinks and spreads south below the surface;
a salinity minimum near 500 m: North Pacific Intermediate Water, fresh water formed far to the north in the subpolar Pacific.

In a T–S diagram each water mass is a bend in the curve.

mean = aloha.mean("time")
smax = mean.salt.sel(depth=slice(0, 300)).idxmax().item()
smin = mean.salt.sel(depth=slice(300, 1000)).idxmin().item()

fig, (ax1, ax2, ax3) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1, 1.3]})
ax1.plot(mean.temp, mean.depth, "o-", color="tab:red", ms=3)
ax1.set(ylim=(1500, 0), xlabel="temperature (°C)", ylabel="depth (m)", title="Temperature")
ax2.plot(mean.salt, mean.depth, "o-", color="tab:blue", ms=3)
ax2.set(ylim=(1500, 0), xlabel="salinity", title="Salinity")
for z, name in [(smax, "S max"), (smin, "S min")]:
    ax2.axhline(z, color="0.5", lw=0.8, ls="--")
    ax2.text(34.2, z - 15, f"{name}, {z:.0f} m", fontsize=9)

d = aloha.depth.broadcast_like(aloha.temp)
sc = ax3.scatter(aloha.salt, aloha.temp, c=d, s=4, cmap="viridis_r", vmin=0, vmax=1500)
ax3.plot(mean.salt, mean.temp, "k-", lw=1)
for z, name, xy in [(smax, "N. Pacific\nTropical Water", (34.3, 26)),
                    (smin, "N. Pacific\nIntermediate Water", (34.6, 10))]:
    ax3.annotate(name, (mean.salt.sel(depth=z), mean.temp.sel(depth=z)), xytext=xy,
                 fontsize=9, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
ax3.set(xlabel="salinity", ylabel="potential temperature (°C)", title="T–S, all 144 profiles")
fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax3, label="depth (m)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








The scatter at the warm end is the seasonal and year-to-year change in the surface water; below about 300 m the 144 profiles fall in a narrow band, because deep water changes slowly.
This is a data-assimilating model reanalysis, not observations. To check it, compare with the HOT program’s own ALOHA profiles.

Each example opens a large ocean dataset as a virtual Icechunk store and answers one question with it in a few seconds or minutes. You download nothing in advance, even when the dataset is hundreds of terabytes or thousands of files. Try your own questions
The examples are starting points. Each store holds far more than one notebook uses. Here are some questions to try:

HYCOM: how does the Bering Sea cold pool’s extent change from year to year? How do currents through the Aleutian passes vary?

GOBAI: is the oxygen minimum zone of the Arabian Sea or off Peru changing too? Where does nitrate track oxygen?

Its data are virtual references to NOAA’s files, so authorize anonymous reads of the store’s virtual chunk containers. List its groups and variables, and explain how the arrays are chunked.

Two parts of that prompt do most of the work:

title: Bonus: forecast model run collections
section: A new run every few hours
text:
A new run every few hours
If we have time and interest. Operational models write a new forecast run on a schedule. Each file is a time series of valid times: when the model says things will happen.

Join the files end to end, and the older runs are lost. Every update means trimming and rewriting the tail
But people ask for different things: the latest forecast, one specific run, or a best estimate, a continuous series that uses the newest run for every hour
To answer all three, the store must keep every run


This expands the slide in lecture 1. A run is also called a cycle, or a forecast model run collection (FMRC) once you keep them all. The skill is building-fmrc-virtual-icechunk in ocean-icechunks-skills.

title: Bonus: forecast model run collections
text:
Two time dimensions








Dimension
Meaning
Values




time
forecast reference time: when the run started
one per run, appended


step
lead time: hours after the run started
the same in every run




Data variables are (time, step, ...), with one chunk per run
Valid time is time + step. It is computed when you read, never stored


Appending a new run adds one entry along time. Nothing already in the store is rewritten.


Do not flatten this to a single valid-time dimension, with each new file appended after the last. That is a different product, a best-estimate series. It discards the older runs.

title: Bonus: forecast model run collections
text:
Our example: GoMOFS

3 runs: 10 to 12 November 2026, 00Z
75 NetCDF files, 55 GB, left in place
401 kB Icechunk store

NOAA’s Gulf of Maine model runs four times a day. Each run is 25 files: the nowcast valid at the run time, and a forecast every 3 hours out to 72 hours.

Numbers from running the notebook on 2026-11-17. The files are NOAA’s public GoMOFS output (noaa-nos-ofs-pds). We use the 00Z run of three days, to keep the notebook quick. The nowcast file n006 is valid at the run time, so it is lead 0.

title: Bonus: forecast model run collections
text:
1 · One run becomes (time, step)
# ds: the 25 files of one run, joined along the valid time (ocean_time)
ref = pd.Timestamp(cycle)                         # the run's reference time
valid = pd.DatetimeIndex(ds["ocean_time"].values)

ds = ds.rename_dims(ocean_time="step").drop_vars("ocean_time")
ds = ds.assign_coords(step=("step", (valid - ref).values))      # lead time

varying = [v for v in ds.data_vars if "step" in ds[v].dims]
static = ds.drop_vars(varying)                                  # grid, mask, ...
ds = xr.merge([ds[varying].expand_dims(time=[np.datetime64(ref)]), static],
              compat="override", combine_attrs="override")

An excerpt of open_cycle in the notebook gomofs-fmrc-icechunk. The notebook also checks that the valid times in the files agree with the times in the file names, so the step axis cannot lie.

title: Bonus: forecast model run collections
text:
Where runs go wrong

Static variables. Grid and mask variables, like h and mask_rho, have no time. Add time only to variables that vary with step. Otherwise every run stores its own copy of the grid
Time encoding. Pin the units of time and step. Left to xarray, they depend on each run’s own values, and a run appended later can decode to the wrong date
Same steps in every run. step is one shared dimension. Check the lead times match before combining, with a clear error
Reference time from the file. Use the file’s own first time, not the date in its name. File names can be off by a day


The first two are the ones people hit. A static variable stacked per run looks fine until you notice the store is much larger than expected, and a wrongly encoded append gives dates that are off with no error.

title: Bonus: forecast model run collections
text:
2 · Create, then append
def commit_cycle(repo, cycle, ds, append):
    session = repo.writable_session("main")
    if append:
        ds_time = ds.drop_vars([v for v in ds.variables if "time" not in ds[v].dims])
        ds_time.vz.to_icechunk(session.store, append_dim="time")
    else:
        ds.vz.to_icechunk(session.store)
    session.commit(f"GoMOFS cycle {cycle:%Y-%m-%d %Hz}")

commit_cycle(repo, first, one_cycle, append=False)     # create
commit_cycle(repo, second, open_cycle(second, cycles[second]), append=True)   # append

One commit per run. An append carries only the variables that have a time dimension, because writing the static variables again would rewrite their metadata, which VirtualiZarr refuses. open_cycle takes a run’s reference time and its files: it is the reshaping on the previous slides, applied to the next run.

title: Bonus: forecast model run collections
section: 3 · Daily updates: diff on reference time
text:
3 · Daily updates: diff on reference time
ds = xr.open_zarr(repo.readonly_session("main").store, consolidated=False, chunks={})

set_repo = set(pd.to_datetime(ds.time.values).strftime("%Y%m%d"))   # runs in the store
new = sorted(set_cloud - set_repo)                                  # only in the bucket

Compare reference times, so a rerun never adds a run twice
Append in increasing time order, so sort the new runs first


set_cloud is the set of complete runs found in the bucket, keyed the same way, as in section 1 of the notebook. If the bucket’s folder dates differ from the reference time, apply that offset in one place and comment on it. Run on the store from the notebook with a fourth run in the bucket, it returns just the fourth run.

title: Bonus: forecast model run collections
section: 4 · Read it: best estimate with Rolodex
text:
4 · Read it: best estimate with Rolodex
import rolodex.forecast
from rolodex.forecast import BestEstimate, ForecastIndex

ds.coords["valid_time"] = rolodex.forecast.create_lazy_valid_time_variable(
    reference_time=ds.time, period=ds.step)                    # time + step
fmrc = ds.drop_indexes(["time", "step"]).set_xindex(
    ["time", "step", "valid_time"], ForecastIndex)

best = fmrc.sel(valid_time=BestEstimate(offset=6))   # newest run for every hour

Rolodex (github.com/dcherian/rolodex) adds an xarray index. offset=6 starts each run at step 6, which is 18 hours in with 3-hour steps, so the first hours of every run, while the model settles, are skipped. The result has one dimension, valid_time, and time and step say which run and lead each value came from. For our three runs it has 35 valid times. The notebook pins Rolodex to commit 527bd42; main was the same commit on 2026-11-17.

What the agent needs from you
It cannot guess these. Put them in your first prompt:

Where the files are, and how to get in: a bucket, a THREDDS catalog, an API; public or which credentials

What the skill works out from your files
It will propose these, and ask you to confirm:

One store, or several? The goal is one store with all the variables. Files on different grids or encodings force groups or separate stores

Authenticating to your bucket
The agent writes to your bucket with your credentials. Tell it where they are:







Destination
Typical credentials




Amazon S3
An AWS profile, or AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in the environment


Google Cloud Storage
A service-account key file, named in GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS

title: The basic pipeline
text:
Six steps









Step
What happens




1
Find the files
List the NetCDF files you want in the store


2
Say how to reach them
An object store, a registry and a parser for the file format


3
Open one file virtually
Read its metadata only. The big arrays stay where they are


4
Combine compatible files
Join them along time into one virtual dataset


5
Write and commit
Save the chunk references to an Icechunk repository


6
Reopen and read
Open the store as a reader would, and read real values




This is exactly the NDVI notebook from chapter 1, so anyone who ran it has already done all six steps. The code on the next slides was run end to end on 2026-11-13 (icechunk 2.3.1, virtualizarr 2.8.0).

title: The basic pipeline
text:
1 · Find the files
import s3fs

fs = s3fs.S3FileSystem(anon=True)          # public bucket, no credentials
urls = [f"s3://{p}" for p in sorted(fs.ls("noaa-cdr-ndvi-pds/data/2000"))[:5]]
Five daily files of the NOAA AVHRR NDVI Climate Data Record, January 1–5, 2000.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
2 · Say how to reach them
from obstore.store import from_url
from obspec_utils.registry import ObjectStoreRegistry
from virtualizarr.parsers import HDFParser

bucket = "s3://noaa-cdr-ndvi-pds/"
store = from_url(bucket, region="us-east-1", skip_signature=True)
registry = ObjectStoreRegistry({bucket: store})   # URLs starting with bucket -> this store
parser = HDFParser()                              # NetCDF4 is HDF5 inside

Pick the parser that matches the file format: HDFParser for NetCDF4/HDF5, NetCDF3Parser for classic NetCDF, and others for DMR++, Zarr and FITS. The audit in chapter 4 tells you which one.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
3 · Open one file virtually
from virtualizarr import open_virtual_dataset

coords = ["time", "latitude", "longitude"]
vds = open_virtual_dataset(url=urls[0], parser=parser, registry=registry,
                           loadable_variables=coords)
NDVI   (time, latitude, longitude) int16 52MB ManifestArray<shape=(1, 3600, 7200) ...>

Small coordinates are loaded. Big arrays become ManifestArrays: lists of where each chunk sits (file, byte offset, length). No data is downloaded.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
4 · Combine compatible files
import xarray as xr

vds_list = [
    open_virtual_dataset(url=u, parser=parser, registry=registry, loadable_variables=coords)
    .drop_vars(["nv", "ncrs", "crs"], errors="ignore")
    for u in urls
]
combined = xr.concat(vds_list, dim="time", data_vars="minimal", coords="minimal",
                     compat="override", combine_attrs="override")

“Compatible” means the same dimensions, shape apart from time, chunk grid, dtype and codecs. Files that differ cannot share one virtual array. The keyword arguments stop xarray from trying to compare virtual arrays, which it cannot do. The dropped variables are small CRS and bounds-dimension variables that get in the way of the join.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
5 · Write and commit
import icechunk

config = icechunk.RepositoryConfig.default()
config.set_virtual_chunk_container(icechunk.VirtualChunkContainer(
    url_prefix=bucket, store=icechunk.s3_store(region="us-east-1", anonymous=True)))

storage = icechunk.local_filesystem_storage("ndvi-icechunk")
repo = icechunk.Repository.create(storage, config)
repo.save_config()
combined["time"].encoding["chunks"] = (len(combined.time),)   # one chunk for time
session = repo.writable_session("main")
combined.vz.to_icechunk(session.store)
session.commit("Five days of NDVI CDR, January 2000")

The virtual chunk container tells Icechunk that some chunks live outside the store, under this prefix, and how to reach them. save_config makes that setting part of the store, so readers get it too. Commits work like git: each one is a snapshot you can go back to.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
6 · Reopen and read real data
creds = icechunk.containers_credentials(
    {bucket: icechunk.s3_credentials(anonymous=True)})
reader = icechunk.Repository.open(icechunk.local_filesystem_storage("ndvi-icechunk"),
                                  authorize_virtual_chunk_access=creds)
ds = xr.open_zarr(reader.readonly_session("main").store, consolidated=False, chunks={})

ds["NDVI"].sel(latitude=slice(50, 40), longitude=slice(-126, -114)).isel(time=0).plot()

Always check from a fresh read-only session, and read real values, not just metadata. That is the reader’s path, and it is where problems show up.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
section: Users want a product, not a pile of files
text:
Users want a product, not a pile of files


A cloud-optimized dataset that is linked to the underlying files hides the file structure. The user opens one dataset, with every variable and the full time range, and never sees a file name. We deliver a product.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
section: Why not just download the files, or use THREDDS?
text:
Why not just download the files, or use THREDDS?


Downloading

Gigabytes to get the one slice you need
Copies on every laptop, all out of date
Hours of scripting before any science

Data servers

Cap large requests (PSL THREDDS: 500 MB each)
Fail under load (“NetCDF: DAP failure”)


Object storage (S3, Google Cloud, Azure)

Serves byte ranges, not whole files
Spreads requests across many machines, so parallel readers do not queue behind each other
In practice, as many connections as you can throw at it



THREDDS has one server, and every request goes through it. Object storage is built to serve huge numbers of concurrent requests for pieces of objects. That is what a cloud-optimized reader needs.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
text:
From minutes to seconds


Resampling a 2-D CEFI MOM6 NEP variable: THREDDS vs. a virtual store in Earthmover Arraylake. Holmes, ESIP, July 2026.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
text:
Bering Sea snow crab, 1994–2015
306 TB of HYCOM reanalysis · opens in ~1 s · nothing downloaded






Open in Colab →

Run all cells. The map is the cold pool on the eastern Bering Sea shelf. The time series is the box-mean bottom temperature and the fraction of the box below 2 °C. The metadata comes from Source Cooperative, and every value is read by byte range from HYCOM’s NetCDF files on AWS Open Data.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
text:
VirtualiZarr: no reprocessing

Keep the data as it is. The NetCDF files stay where the provider put them.
Build a catalog of chunks. For every chunk: which file, at what byte offset, and how long.
Save the catalog as one Zarr dataset. Readers open that, and read the bytes straight from the original files.


If the files are compatible (the same grid, chunking and encoding), there is nothing to rewrite.


This is the big change. We used to have to convert everything to Zarr, which meant a second copy of petabytes. Virtual references point at the originals.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
text:
Why Icechunk, not Kerchunk?
Kerchunk made virtual datasets possible. Icechunk makes them safe to share and keep up to date.

Transactions. Commits are atomic, with snapshots and rollback. Kerchunk references are plain JSON or Parquet files that anyone can overwrite.
Safe appends. New files are added in a commit, and readers never see a half-written store. With Kerchunk you rewrite the references yourself.
Zarr-native. The store is a real Zarr store, so any Zarr reader opens it. Kerchunk needs an extra fsspec reference layer.
Scale. Chunk manifests are built for huge chunk counts. Very large JSON reference sets are slow to load.
Modern I/O. The stack reads through Rust and obstore, not fsspec: more flexible (S3, GCS, Azure, local, HTTP) and fast under many concurrent requests.


Kerchunk was the first way to get a virtual dataset, and it is still fine for a quick one-off. The problems show up when a dataset is shared and grows: there is no versioning, no atomic update, and no protection from two writers.
On I/O: Icechunk’s Rust core uses the Rust object_store crate. obstore is the Python binding to the same crate, and VirtualiZarr uses it to read NetCDF metadata (the ObjectStoreRegistry in the notebook). Kerchunk goes through fsspec. obstore’s own benchmarks show large gains over fsspec for many concurrent requests; say “in our experience” unless you have timed your own case.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
text:
Handling forecast model run collections
A forecast model writes a new file every day. Keep every run, not just the latest.

Two time dimensions. time is the forecast reference time, one value per file. step is the lead time, the same in every file. Data are (time, step, ...).
Append along time. Each new file adds one entry. Nothing is rewritten.
Valid time is computed. It is time + step, never stored.
Pick a run, or a best estimate. Select one forecast, or stitch the newest hours from every run into one continuous series.


One store holds the whole history of every forecast. Bonus lecture 7 builds one.


The raw files each have a single time dimension of valid times. If we simply join them end to end, we throw away the older runs, and every update means trimming and rewriting the tail. Splitting time into the reference time and the lead time keeps every run, and a daily update is one append.
In the agent skill (building-fmrc-virtual-icechunk), the reshaping is done per file before the concat: rename the time dimension to step, make the first valid time the scalar reference time, then concatenate along time. All files must have the same number of steps. Static variables (bathymetry, mesh connectivity) must be kept out of the concat, or they get stacked once per run.
Best estimate is computed at read time, with Rolodex. Worked example: the Taranto SHYFEM forecast store in the MAGICA school notebooks.

text:
Write, list, read and delete
import s3fs

title: The scratch bucket
section: An Icechunk store in the scratch bucket
text:
An Icechunk store in the scratch bucket
You can write an Icechunk store here almost as easily as to a local folder. Only the storage setup changes:
import boto3
import icechunk

bucket, prefix = scratch.removeprefix("s3://").split("/", 1)
creds = boto3.Session().get_credentials().get_frozen_credentials()   # the hub's credentials

storage = icechunk.s3_storage(
    bucket=bucket,
    prefix=f"{prefix}/my-store",
    region="us-west-2",
    access_key_id=creds.access_key,
    secret_access_key=creds.secret_key,
    session_token=creds.token,
)






Note



Why not from_env=True? On this hub, Icechunk does not pick up the hub’s credentials by itself, and you get AccessDenied (tested 2026-11-13 with icechunk 2.3.1). Passing them from boto3 works. They expire after about an hour, so rerun the cell if a long session starts failing.

title: Auditing your files
section: A virtual store is only as consistent as its files
text:
A virtual store is only as consistent as its files
Nothing is rewritten, so the files’ layout is the store’s layout.

A virtual store copies no data. So it can fix metadata, but it cannot fix how the bytes are laid out: the grid, the chunks, the compression. An audit tells you, before you build, whether the files will make a good store, a slow one, or several stores.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Consistent grids

Same dimensions, shape and coordinate values in every file, apart from the time dimension you join along
Files on different grids cannot share one array. They become separate groups, or separate stores


CoastWatch Ocean Heat Content: three regions on three different lat/lon grids, so three separate stores.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Consistent chunking

A chunk is the smallest piece a reader can fetch. Virtual stores keep the provider’s chunks exactly
Every file needs the same chunk shape for a variable
Unchunked arrays mean every read pulls the whole array


NOAA NDVI: NDVI is chunked 1 × 1200 × 2400, but QA in the same file is unchunked, so any read of QA pulls all 3600 × 7200 values.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Consistent encoding

Same dtype, compression, fill value and file format in every file
NetCDF-3 and NetCDF-4/HDF5 need different parsers, and cannot be mixed in one array
Check the file’s own header. Catalogs and servers get this wrong


PacIOOS: the servers implied HDF5, but the files were NetCDF-3. About 3,200 “replacement” files were compressed HDF5 under the same names.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Built to be appended

New files arrive the same way: same naming, same folder pattern, same grid
Each file’s length along time is a whole number of chunks. If not, an append can put data in the wrong place without any error
One time step per file works, but the time coordinate needs explicit chunking or the store opens slowly


CEFI daily files: 365 or 366 days each, chunked 100 days. In a test with that layout, appending put 430 of 730 values in the wrong place, with no error.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Bugs in the data

Missing time steps. Is it a real gap, or the product’s normal cadence?
Duplicated or out-of-order time steps
Empty, truncated or unreadable files
Coordinates that are all zero or all NaN


HYCOM GOFS 3.1: a few analyses are missing from the archive, so the snow crab notebook takes the nearest time that exists.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Missing or wrong metadata
This is the one thing a virtual store can fix, without touching the data.

Missing units, standard_name, long_name, or a vertical positive
Attributes that cannot be saved as JSON, such as a NaN fill value on a coordinate
No version recorded anywhere in the files


Fix it in the store, write down every change, and make the result follow CF conventions.

Which stores cover my place and period?
If we have time and interest. The ocean-icechunks account holds many stores. To pick the right ones, describe each store in a catalog you can search.

text:
Map: Bering Sea bottom temperature
water_temp_bottom is the temperature at the sea floor — the water crabs actually sit in. The Bering Sea straddles the dateline and the store runs −180…180, so take the two sides separately and put them together on a 0–360 longitude axis. (Each side is .load()ed before joining: xr.concat on the lazy store would otherwise try to read everything.)
On the map, the blue tongue on the shelf inside the black 2 °C line is the cold pool. The deep basin to the southwest is also just under 2 °C, so the same line traces the shelf break as well.

when = "2010-07-15T12"   # mid-July, when NOAA's summer bottom-trawl survey is at sea

da = ds.water_temp_bottom.sel(time=when, lat=slice(50, 67))
bering = xr.concat([da.sel(lon=slice(160, 180)).load(),
                    da.sel(lon=slice(-180, -155)).load()], dim="lon")
bering = bering.assign_coords(lon=bering.lon % 360)   # 160°E … 205° (= 155°W)

# The snow crab box used below: eastern Bering Sea middle/outer shelf.
box = dict(lat=(57, 61), lon=(-173, -165))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
bering.plot(ax=ax, cmap="RdYlBu_r", vmin=-2, vmax=10,
            cbar_kwargs={"label": "bottom temperature (°C)"})
bering.plot.contour(ax=ax, levels=[2], colors="k", linewidths=0.8)   # the 2 °C "cold pool" edge
ax.add_patch(mpatches.Rectangle((box["lon"][0] % 360, box["lat"][0]),
                                box["lon"][1] - box["lon"][0], box["lat"][1] - box["lat"][0],
                                fill=False, ec="magenta", lw=2))
ax.set(title=f"HYCOM bottom temperature, {when[:10]} (black: 2 °C; magenta: snow crab box)",
       xlabel="longitude (°E, 0–360)", ylabel="latitude")

section: Time series: bottom temperature on the snow crab grounds
text:
Time series: bottom temperature on the snow crab grounds
Snow crab live on the eastern Bering Sea shelf in cold bottom water; the juveniles depend on the cold pool, water below 2 °C left on the bottom after winter sea ice. Here is one mid-July snapshot per year, 1994–2015, over the box above: the box-mean bottom temperature and the fraction of the box inside the cold pool.
Each snapshot is the 12Z analysis nearest 15 July (a few analyses are missing from the archive, so the nearest present one is used). Note that any read inside a map fetches the whole 29 MB global level, so this is 22 reads, about 0.6 GB — seconds in AWS us-west-2, somewhat longer elsewhere. A long daily or 3-hourly series would be thousands of reads.

import dask, numpy as np

analyses = ds.time[(ds.tau == 0).values]          # 12Z analyses that exist in the archive
times = [analyses.sel(time=f"{y}-07-15T12", method="nearest").values for y in range(1994, 2016)]

crab = ds.water_temp_bottom.sel(time=times, lat=slice(*box["lat"]), lon=slice(*box["lon"]))
crab = crab.chunk({"time": 1})                    # stream one time step at a time, in parallel
weights = np.cos(np.deg2rad(crab.lat))            # grid cells shrink toward the pole

ocean = crab.notnull()
mean_temp = crab.weighted(weights).mean(["lat", "lon"])
cold_frac = (crab < 2).where(ocean).weighted(weights).mean(["lat", "lon"])
mean_temp, cold_frac = dask.compute(mean_temp, cold_frac)

title: NCEI OA indicators: the aragonite saturation horizon
text: A textbook ocean acidification picture from NCEI’s climatology of ocean acidification indicators on the North American margins (1° grid, surface to 500 m, observations 2003–2018 adjusted to 2010), as a virtual Icechunk store. No credentials needed. Runs on Google Colab (Python 3.12).

title: NCEI OA indicators: the aragonite saturation horizon
text:
The textbook idea
The ocean takes up about a quarter of the CO₂ that people emit. Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which lowers pH and uses up carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻), the building block that corals, pteropods, oysters and other animals use to make shells of calcium carbonate.
The aragonite saturation state, ΩA, measures how easy that is:
\[\Omega_A = \frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]\,[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]}{K'_{sp}}\]

ΩA > 1: seawater is supersaturated, and aragonite shells can form and persist.
ΩA < 1: seawater is corrosive, and unprotected aragonite dissolves.

ΩA falls with depth. Deep water is cold and under pressure, both of which make aragonite more soluble, and it holds CO₂ released by the decay of sinking organic matter. The depth where ΩA = 1 is the aragonite saturation horizon. Two things set how deep it is:

Ocean basin. North Pacific deep water is old and has collected respired CO₂ for centuries, so its horizon is far shallower than the North Atlantic’s.
Upwelling. Along the US West Coast, spring and summer winds bring that corrosive water up onto the continental shelf (Feely et al. 2008). It was behind the oyster-hatchery failures in the Pacific Northwest (Barton et al. 2012), and every bit of anthropogenic CO₂ raises the horizon further.

Why the store helps
NCEI ships this product as one NetCDF file per indicator, and the files’ latitude, longitude and depth axes are placeholder zeros, so you cannot select a place or draw a map without rebuilding the grid by hand. The store puts all 12 indicators on one real (depth, lat, lon) grid.

title: NCEI OA indicators: the aragonite saturation horizon
text:
Map the saturation horizon
OmegaA_an is the analysed aragonite saturation state, 1.2 MB for the whole 3-D field. For each grid cell, find the shallowest depth where it drops below 1.

omega = ds.OmegaA_an.load()

corrosive = omega < 1
horizon = corrosive.idxmax("depth").where(corrosive.any("depth"))   # first depth with Ω < 1
not_reached = omega.notnull().any("depth") & ~corrosive.any("depth")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
ax.set_facecolor("0.9")                                   # land, and cells with no data
not_reached.where(not_reached).plot(ax=ax, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=3, add_colorbar=False)
horizon.plot(ax=ax, cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=500,
             cbar_kwargs={"label": "depth where Ω_A first falls below 1 (m)"})
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(color=plt.cm.Blues(1 / 3), label="Ω_A > 1 at every sampled depth"),
                   Patch(color="0.9", label="land or no data")],
          loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.12), ncols=2)
ax.set(title="Aragonite saturation horizon", xlabel="longitude", ylabel="latitude",
       xlim=(-180, -40), ylim=(10, 75))
plt.show()









Pacific coast, Mexico to Alaska: corrosive water sits only 100–150 m down, on or just off the shelf. Offshore, in the subtropical gyre, the horizon deepens to 400 m and below 500 m.
Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean: ΩA stays above 1 at every depth sampled, down to 500 m.
Two shallow spots: off southern Mexico and Central America, where an oxygen-poor, CO₂-rich layer lies close under the surface, and Hudson Bay, whose river-fed water is low in carbonate; in both, ΩA is below 1 within 10–50 m of the surface.

title: NCEI OA indicators: the aragonite saturation horizon

Oregon’s shelf edge against the open Gulf of Mexico. Both start supersaturated at the surface; only one crosses ΩA = 1.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
for name, lat, lon in [("Oregon", 44.5, -125.5), ("Gulf of Mexico", 26.5, -90.5)]:

    ax.plot(p, p.depth, "o-", label=name)

Caveats. This is a climatology: observations from 2003–2018, adjusted to the year 2010 and gridded at 1°, so it smooths seasons and upwelling events, and the horizon is only as fine as the depth levels (100, 125, 150 m …). OmegaA_dd gives the number of observations behind each cell, useful for judging where the map is well constrained.
More: the store’s README lists all 72 variables (pH, DIC, alkalinity, pCO₂, Revelle factor, …) and how to cite the data.

title: OISST: marine heatwaves in the Gulf of Maine
text:
The Gulf of Maine is one of the fastest-warming patches of ocean on Earth, and its 2012 marine heatwave upended the lobster season (Mills et al. 2013). Here we count marine heatwave days in every year since 1982, from NOAA’s daily OISST v2.1.
That takes the full daily record, about 16,500 NetCDF files. The virtual Icechunk store, maintained by NERACOOS / GMRI, makes them one dataset, so it is one sel(). No credentials needed.

section: What counts as a marine heatwave
text:
What counts as a marine heatwave
The standard definition (Hobday et al. 2016): a marine heatwave is at least 5 days in a row when the temperature is above the 90th percentile for that day of the year, measured against a 30-year baseline. Here the baseline is 1991–2020, and the percentile is smoothed with a 31-day running mean (a slight simplification of Hobday’s method).

title: OISST: marine heatwaves in the Gulf of Maine
section: Every day since 1981, averaged over the Gulf of Maine
text:
Every day since 1981, averaged over the Gulf of Maine
A box from 42 to 44.5 °N and 70.5 to 66 °W; land reads as NaN and drops out of the mean. Each chunk in NOAA’s files is a whole global map, so even this small box reads every file once. It took about 3 minutes on a JupyterHub in AWS; elsewhere, including Colab, expect longer.
With 16,500 requests, a dropped connection now and then is likely, and one is enough to stop a single big read. So read a year at a time, and try a year again if it fails.

box = daily.sst.squeeze("zlev").sel(lat=slice(42, 44.5), lon=slice(289.5, 294))

def read_year(year, tries=3):
    for attempt in range(tries):
        try:
            return box.sel(time=str(year)).mean(["lat", "lon"]).load()
        except Exception as err:          # usually a dropped connection: try again
            print(f"{year}: attempt {attempt + 1} failed ({type(err).__name__})")
    raise RuntimeError(f"could not read {year}")

start = time.time()
gom = xr.concat([read_year(y) for y in range(1981, daily.time.dt.year.values[-1] + 1)], dim="time")
print(f"{gom.time.size:,} days read in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")

title: OISST: marine heatwaves in the Gulf of Maine
text:
Find the heatwave days

base = gom.sel(time=slice("1991", "2020")).groupby("time.dayofyear")

def smooth(c):   # 31-day running mean, wrapping around the new year
    return c.pad(dayofyear=15, mode="wrap").rolling(dayofyear=31, center=True).mean()[15:-15]

clim = smooth(base.mean())
p90 = smooth(base.quantile(0.9)).drop_vars("quantile")

doy = gom.time.dt.dayofyear
hot = (gom > p90.sel(dayofyear=doy)).to_series()
run = hot.ne(hot.shift()).cumsum()                         # number each run of hot / not-hot days
heatwave = hot & hot.groupby(run).transform("size").ge(5)  # keep runs of 5 days or more
days_per_year = heatwave.groupby(heatwave.index.year).sum().loc[1982:]


fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 8))

y = "2012"
one = gom.sel(time=y)
ax1.plot(one.time, one, color="k", lw=1, label=f"{y} daily SST")
ax1.plot(one.time, clim.sel(dayofyear=one.time.dt.dayofyear), color="tab:blue", label="1991–2020 mean")
ax1.plot(one.time, p90.sel(dayofyear=one.time.dt.dayofyear), color="tab:blue", ls="--", label="90th percentile")
ax1.fill_between(one.time, p90.sel(dayofyear=one.time.dt.dayofyear), one,
                 where=heatwave.loc[y].values, color="tab:red", alpha=0.6, label="heatwave")
ax1.set(ylabel="SST (°C)", title=f"Gulf of Maine, {y}")
ax1.legend(loc="upper left")

ax2.bar(days_per_year.index, days_per_year, color="tab:red")
ax2.set(xlabel="year", ylabel="heatwave days",
        title=f"Marine heatwave days per year ({days_per_year.index[-1]} is a partial year)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








In 2012 (top) the Gulf of Maine sat above its 90th percentile for most of the year: 246 heatwave days. Before 2010, heatwaves here were rare, about 3 days a year on average and never more than 20. Since 2010 the average is 93 days a year, with 2021 (238 days) close to 2012. 2024–2026 have been calmer so far.
One caution: the baseline is fixed at 1991–2020, so a steadily warming ocean shows up as more heatwave days. Hobday et al. discuss this; detrending first, or a moving baseline, separates short extremes from the long-term warming.
